objectives.statement: Use the particle model to describe and compare solids, liquids and gases (arrangement, movement, shape and volume), with Liberian examples.
Explain melting, freezing, evaporation, boiling and condensation as energy gained or lost by particles, and distinguish evaporation from boiling.
Predict and explain, with evidence, what happens to temperature when ice melts in a drink (it stays at about 0 °C while ice remains), and recognise changes of state as reversible physical changes.

content.body: Synthetic water-model demonstration at approximately one atmosphere. Predict first. The simulation simplifies a pure substance and is not a safe procedure for heating water. A prediction is a reasoned claim to test, not a fact established by the animation.

accessibility.textAlternative: Synthetic water-model demonstration at approximately one atmosphere. Predict first. The simulation simplifies a pure substance and is not a safe procedure for heating water. A prediction is a reasoned claim to test, not a fact established by the animation. What happens to ice as it warms from -5 degrees C to 20 degrees C? Options: It melts; the particles remain water particles.; The particles themselves grow into liquid particles.. After you predict, the observation is shown. Compare your prediction with the observation and explain the role of energy.

content.body: Keep the substance and pressure fixed while changing temperature. Watch arrangement and motion. Real water can contain ice and liquid together during melting; a temperature slider alone does not model the time or energy needed for that phase change.

accessibility.textAlternative: Keep the substance and pressure fixed while changing temperature. Watch arrangement and motion. Real water can contain ice and liquid together during melting; a temperature slider alone does not model the time or energy needed for that phase change. Change temperature and compare solid, liquid and gas representations. This is a simplified model, not measured data. Below 0 °C water is a solid: particles packed in a pattern, vibrating in place. From 0 °C to 100 °C it is a liquid: particles close together, sliding past one another. At 100 °C and above it is a gas: particles far apart, moving quickly in all directions.

content.body: Worked reasoning: a liquid changes container shape because its particles can move past one another. A solid keeps its shape because its particles remain arranged around fixed positions while vibrating. A gas spreads because its particles are widely spaced and moving freely. Particle identity does not change during these physical changes.

accessibility.textAlternative: Worked reasoning: a liquid changes container shape because its particles can move past one another. A solid keeps its shape because its particles remain arranged around fixed positions while vibrating. A gas spreads because its particles are widely spaced and moving freely. Particle identity does not change during these physical changes. Which explanation fits a liquid changing container shape? Options: Particles move past one another.; The particles turn into a new substance.. Why can ice keep melting at about zero degrees C? Options: Energy changes particle arrangement during melting.; No energy reaches the ice..
